title: How You Can Fix The Mess of Public Education
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that public education has become a mess of toxic coddling — low standards, weak accountability, and permissive frameworks like PBIS, SEL, MTSS, and restorative justice that he claims actively worsen student behavior. His central claim is that individual teachers, not administrators or districts, are the real engine of change, and that change nearly always starts with one teacher rather than a policy memo. The concrete move he recommends is to stop complaining and instead build a small coalition: confide in one trusted colleague, slowly add others, then bring a specific solution (not a grievance) to the principal or superintendent, framed around making their job easier and improving test scores. He contrasts this ground-level path with the disconnect of district and union bureaucrats, whom he accuses of making decisions based on virtue signaling rather than classroom reality. The piece closes as a call to action, insisting that any individual teacher has the power to start reversing the decline through a single honest conversation.
points: Complaining to administration accomplishes nothing; arriving with a concrete solution that promises an easier job and better scores gets a hearing.
Meaningful change in a school almost always starts with a single teacher who first confides in one trusted colleague.
Build a small coalition of like-minded colleagues before approaching the principal, rather than acting alone.
District and union officials are portrayed as disconnected from classrooms, driven more by politics than by what actually works.
quotes: Toxic coddling has destroyed it. There is no “rigor” or accountability. Standards are staggeringly low and students have few boundaries.
Every approved and accepted method of classroom management by the powers that be only makes behavior worse—PBIS, SEL, MTSS, and restorative justice practices to name a few.
Complaining will get you nowhere. Your principal, however, or superintendent would love to hear solutions.
Build a small coalition of like-minded warriors and then bring your solution to the boss.
The truth is, all those bureaucrats in district and union offices and government buildings don’t know a whit about what’s happening on the ground and in classrooms.
It’s tragic and getting worse. And we have yet to see rock bottom. But the power is with you to change it.
